short_summary: Inorganic cluster supramolecular compounds (ICSs) represent an advanced class of materials formed through coordination-driven self-assembly between metal-containing nodes and organic ligands. This comprehensive review examines the foundational design principles, synthesis methodologies, and burgeoning biomedical applications of these complex architectures, which include metallacages, helicates, and metallacycles. By leveraging the predictable nature of metal-ligand coordination and dynamic reversibility, researchers can engineer discrete, thermodynamically stable structures with precise spatial control. The article details advanced experimental protocols, structural characterization techniques such as X-ray crystallography and NMR spectroscopy, and critical optimization strategies for stability and reproducibility. Furthermore, it highlights the significant potential of ICSs in advanced therapeutics, specifically focusing on their use as novel anticancer agents, targeted drug delivery vehicles, and multimodal theranostic platforms. Despite current challenges regarding water solubility and biosafety, the modularity, tunability, and host-guest chemistry capabilities of ICSs position them as highly promising candidates for next-generation pharmaceutical development and personalized medicine.
long_summary: Inorganic cluster supramolecular compounds (ICSs), also known as supramolecular coordination complexes, occupy a strategic intersection between classical supramolecular chemistry and coordination chemistry. Formed via coordination-driven self-assembly of transition metal nodes and multidentate organic linkers, these materials are characterized by their structural precision, tunable cavities, and dynamic reversibility. This comprehensive technical review explores the foundational design principles governing the construction of major ICS classes, including three-dimensional metallacages, chiral helicates, and two-dimensional metallacycles. The rational design of these structures leverages directional bonding, symmetry interaction, and subcomponent self-assembly to create discrete architectures with defined shapes and sizes. The review provides detailed insights into experimental methodologies, emphasizing solvothermal synthesis, microwave-assisted techniques, and mechanochemical approaches. Rigorous characterization using nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, mass spectrometry, and single-crystal X-ray diffraction is essential for verifying phase purity and structural integrity. A critical focus is placed on the precise control of reaction parameters, such as temperature, pH, solvent polarity, and ionic strength, which dictate the thermodynamic and kinetic pathways of self-assembly. Furthermore, the article explores the synergistic effects of non-covalent interactions, particularly hydrogen bonding and π-π stacking, in maintaining framework stability within complex biological environments. In the biomedical domain, ICSs demonstrate exceptional potential as advanced therapeutics. Their unique host-guest chemistry enables the encapsulation of conventional chemotherapeutics, facilitating targeted drug delivery and stimuli-responsive release mechanisms triggered by the tumor microenvironment. Additionally, specific supramolecular metal-based structures exhibit intrinsic anticancer cytotoxicity and can serve as scaffolds for multimodal theranostic agents, combining therapeutic and diagnostic imaging capabilities. While challenges remain regarding aqueous solubility, biocompatibility, and potential heavy metal toxicity, ongoing research into surface engineering, nanocarrier encapsulation, and rational ligand design continues to address these limitations. Ultimately, the modularity and multifunctionality of ICSs offer significant advantages over traditional materials, positioning them at the forefront of innovative drug development and precision medicine.
